newsitem.title: USA: Report on CPI flaws to be watched closely at Fed.
newsitem.headline: Report on CPI flaws to be watched closely at Fed.

text.p: The release of a report on the Consumer Price Index is being watched closely at the Federal Reserve, where policymakers are struggling to get a handle on where they stand in the fight against inflation.

"I think the Fed will be watching and correctly so since they do face a problem in their inflation measures," said Daniel Bachman, economist at the WEFA Group consulting firm in Eddystone, Pennsylvania.
With inflation as currently measured by the CPI running at about 3 percent a year, the report could suggest the Fed is already very close to achieving its goal of price stability.
Bachman said that if the central bank accepts the report's findings, it would indicate a need for caution in attempts to drive inflation much lower than it already is.
"The Fed doesn't want to drive the economy into a situation where prices will actually fall because the measurement they have been using is flawed," he said.

A congressionally appointed panel, led by Stanford University economist Michael Boskin, on Wednesday plans to unveil recommendations for fixing suspected flaws in the government's main inflation gauge.
The report is expected to conclude that the Labor Department's CPI overstates inflation by a percentage point a year or more.

In an interview last week, San Francisco Fed President Robert Parry raised the issue of likely mismeasurements of both inflation and productivity, saying he was looking forward to the Boskin commission's findings on the CPI.

Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan himself became a catalyst to the appointment of the congressionally named mission nearly two years ago when he put a spotlight on the view that the CPI may be overstated.

In the months since that comment, Federal Reserve Board staff economists Matthew Shapiro and David Wilcox have conducted their own study, concluding that the CPI has an upward bias of about 1.1 percentage points a year -- a finding consistent with what the Boskin report is expected to show.

"I think the Boskin report is going to echo what Alan Greenspan has been saying all along -- that the CPI is overstated," said David Wyss, research director at the economic consulting firm DRI/McGraw-Hill.
In testimony to the Senate Finance Committee in early 1995, the Fed Chairman stressed the benefits to the budget of adjusting the CPI.
Aside from the budget, the Fed has other reasons for its interest in attempts to make the CPI more accurate.
"The Fed is trying to make judgments on how strong economic growth is and how much of an inflation risk there is," said economist Charles Lieberman at Chase Securities Inc.

"If the Boskin commission estimates are correct, it means that inflation is better behaved than people had thought and that the Fed has already achieved a degree of price stability it had hoped for in the next recession," Lieberman said.
Lieberman and Bachman, however, both expressed skepticism that an overstatement in the CPI exists to the same extent that the Boskin commission has likely concluded.
Differences of opinion on the subject mean it will probably be discussed a great deal further within the Fed, Bachman said.
